```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
library(caret)
library(randomForest)
library(ggplot2)
pct <- function(x, digits = 1) sprintf("%.*f%%", digits, 100 * x)
```

## Overview

The question is whether wearable sensors can tell a correct dumbbell curl from
four common mistakes. This report cleans the sensor data, compares a single
classification tree with a random forest using 5-fold cross-validation,
estimates the forest's out-of-sample error on a held-back validation set, and
then checks how well the model carries over to a person it has never seen.
The [conclusion](#conclusion) collects the numbers.

## Data

Six participants did sets of ten dumbbell biceps curls in five ways while
sensors on the belt, upper arm, forearm and dumbbell recorded their movement
(Velloso et al., 2013). Class A is the correct technique. The others are
common mistakes: throwing the elbows to the front (B), lifting only halfway
(C), lowering only halfway (D) and throwing the hips to the front (E). Each
row of the data is one reading taken from the continuous sensor stream.

```{r load}
urls <- c("https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-training.csv",
          "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-testing.csv")
files <- file.path("data", basename(urls))
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
for (i in seq_along(urls)) {
  if (!file.exists(files[i])) download.file(urls[i], files[i], mode = "wb")
}

na_strings <- c("NA", "", "#DIV/0!")
raw  <- read.csv(files[1], na.strings = na_strings)
test <- read.csv(files[2], na.strings = na_strings)
dim(raw)
dim(test)
table(raw$classe)
```

## Choosing the predictors

Of the 159 candidate columns, only 52 are usable. Two groups go.

**Window summaries.** The sensors' stream was cut into short time windows, and
100 columns hold statistics for each window (kurtosis, skewness, maximum,
variance and so on). They are filled in only on the
`r sum(raw$new_window == "yes")` rows that close a window and are empty on all
20 test rows, so a model could never use them at prediction time.

```{r missing}
na_share <- colMeans(is.na(raw))
table(cut(na_share, c(-Inf, 0, 0.97, 1),
          labels = c("no missing values", "up to 97% missing", "over 97% missing")))
```

**Bookkeeping columns.** The first seven columns describe the recording, not
the movement, and some of them leak the answer. `X` is the row number, and the
file is sorted by class, so `X` separates the classes perfectly in the training
data and means nothing anywhere else:

```{r leak}
tapply(raw$X, raw$classe, range)
mean(test$num_window %in% raw$num_window)
```

The window number is just as dangerous. Every test row comes from a window
that also appears in the training file, so looking up `num_window` would score
20 out of 20 on the quiz while learning nothing about how anyone lifts. The
timestamps play the same role. The participant's name is dropped too, so the
model has to rely on the sensors.

```{r clean}
bookkeeping <- c("X", "user_name", "raw_timestamp_part_1", "raw_timestamp_part_2",
                 "cvtd_timestamp", "new_window", "num_window")
predictors <- setdiff(names(raw)[na_share == 0], c(bookkeeping, "classe"))
data <- data.frame(raw[predictors], classe = factor(raw$classe))

length(predictors)
length(nearZeroVar(data[predictors]))
```

The 52 predictors that remain are the roll, pitch, yaw and total acceleration
of each of the four sensors, plus their x, y and z gyroscope, accelerometer and
magnetometer readings. None has near-zero variance, so no further filtering is
needed.

## Cross-validation design

The data is used in two layers so that the final error estimate is honest.

1. **A validation set.** 25% of the rows, stratified by class, are set aside
   before any modelling. They are used once, at the end, to estimate the
   out-of-sample error of the chosen model.
2. **5-fold cross-validation** on the other 75% picks the model and tunes it.
   Both models below use the same five folds, so their scores are directly
   comparable.

Five folds is a practical middle ground. Each fold still trains on about
`r format(round(0.75 * 0.8 * nrow(data), -2), big.mark = ",")` rows, so the
estimate is not pessimistic, and it costs half the model fits of 10-fold
cross-validation, which matters for a random forest.

```{r split}
set.seed(2026)
in_fit <- createDataPartition(data$classe, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
fit_set    <- data[in_fit, ]
validation <- data[-in_fit, ]
folds <- createFolds(fit_set$classe, k = 5, returnTrain = TRUE)
ctrl  <- trainControl(method = "cv", index = folds)
c(fit_set = nrow(fit_set), validation = nrow(validation))
```

## Models

**Baseline: a single classification tree.** A tree is easy to read and sets a
floor. Its complexity parameter `cp` is tuned over ten values.

**Main model: a random forest.** The boundaries between the classes are
unlikely to be simple. A mistake such as throwing the hips forward shows up as
a combination of belt, arm and dumbbell movement, and many of the 52 readings
are strongly correlated with each other. A random forest handles nonlinear
boundaries, interactions and correlated inputs without scaling or feature
engineering, and averaging many trees makes it far more stable than one tree.
The number of predictors tried at each split, `mtry`, is tuned over 2, 7 (close
to the usual default of √52), 14 and 27. Each forest has 150 trees.

```{r models}
tree_fit <- train(classe ~ ., data = fit_set, method = "rpart",
                  tuneLength = 10, trControl = ctrl)

set.seed(2026)
rf_fit <- train(classe ~ ., data = fit_set, method = "rf", ntree = 150,
                tuneGrid = data.frame(mtry = c(2, 7, 14, 27)), trControl = ctrl)
```

```{r cv-table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = c("Classification tree", "Random forest"),
  best_setting = c(sprintf("cp = %.4f", tree_fit$bestTune$cp),
                   sprintf("mtry = %d", rf_fit$bestTune$mtry)),
  cv_accuracy = pct(c(max(tree_fit$results$Accuracy), max(rf_fit$results$Accuracy)), 2)
), col.names = c("Model", "Best setting", "5-fold CV accuracy"))
```

The tree gets `r pct(max(tree_fit$results$Accuracy), 0)` of the readings
right and the forest almost all of them, so the forest is the model carried
forward. Figure 1 shows that `mtry` barely matters. Every value tried scores at
least `r pct(min(rf_fit$results$Accuracy), 1)`, and the best and worst differ
by `r round(100 * diff(range(rf_fit$results$Accuracy)), 2)` percentage points
(note the narrow y axis). The forest's own out-of-bag error is already
`r pct(rf_fit$finalModel$err.rate[50, "OOB"], 2)` at 50 trees and
`r pct(rf_fit$finalModel$err.rate[150, "OOB"], 2)` at 150, so more trees would
not change the result.

```{r fig-mtry, fig.cap = "Figure 1. Cross-validated accuracy of the random forest for each value of mtry."}
ggplot(rf_fit) +
  labs(x = "Predictors tried at each split (mtry)", y = "5-fold CV accuracy") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Figure 2 shows which readings the forest leans on most.

```{r fig-importance, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Figure 2. The 15 most important predictors (mean decrease in Gini impurity, scaled to 100)."}
importance <- varImp(rf_fit)
top_three <- head(rownames(importance$importance)[order(-importance$importance$Overall)], 3)
plot(importance, top = 15, xlab = "Relative importance")
```

The three most important are `r knitr::combine_words(top_three, before = "\x60")`.

## Expected out-of-sample error

The chosen forest now predicts the validation set, which played no part in
fitting or tuning.

```{r validate}
cm <- confusionMatrix(predict(rf_fit, validation), validation$classe)
cm$table

accuracy    <- unname(cm$overall["Accuracy"])
accuracy_ci <- unname(cm$overall[c("AccuracyLower", "AccuracyUpper")])
oos_error   <- 1 - accuracy
tree_accuracy <- mean(predict(tree_fit, validation) == validation$classe)
```

Validation accuracy is **`r pct(accuracy, 2)`**, so the estimated
out-of-sample error is **`r pct(oos_error, 2)`**, with a 95% confidence
interval of `r pct(1 - accuracy_ci[2], 2)` to `r pct(1 - accuracy_ci[1], 2)`.
Sensitivity is between `r pct(min(cm$byClass[, "Sensitivity"]), 1)` and
`r pct(max(cm$byClass[, "Sensitivity"]), 1)` across the five classes, so no
single mistake type is being missed. The cross-validation estimate,
`r pct(max(rf_fit$results$Accuracy), 2)`, agrees, which is a sign the model
was not overfitted to the folds. The tree, for comparison, scores
`r pct(tree_accuracy, 1)` on the same rows.

With an error rate this low, the chance of getting all 20 test cases right is
roughly (1 − `r round(oos_error, 4)`)^20^ ≈ `r pct((1 - oos_error)^20, 0)`.

One caveat shapes how far this number reaches. The readings are a continuous
stream, so for almost every validation row, the readings taken a split second
before and after it are in the training set. That makes the task easier than
classifying a fresh recording. It is also exactly the situation of the 20 test
cases, whose windows all appear in the training data, so the estimate is the
right one for them.

## How well does this carry over to a new person?

To see how the model would do on someone it has never seen, the forest is
refitted six times, each time leaving out one participant entirely and then
predicting that person's readings. It uses the tuned `mtry` and 150 trees.

```{r loso}
subjects <- raw$user_name
set.seed(2026)
loso_accuracy <- sapply(sort(unique(subjects)), function(s) {
  held_out <- subjects == s
  model <- randomForest(classe ~ ., data = data[!held_out, ], ntree = 150,
                        mtry = rf_fit$bestTune$mtry)
  mean(predict(model, data[held_out, ]) == data$classe[held_out])
})
always_a <- tapply(data$classe == "A", subjects, mean)
round(rbind(forest = loso_accuracy, always_guess_A = always_a), 3)
```

```{r fig-loso, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Figure 3. Accuracy on each participant when that participant is left out of training. The dashed line is the validation accuracy for known participants."}
ggplot(data.frame(subject = names(loso_accuracy), accuracy = loso_accuracy),
       aes(reorder(subject, accuracy), accuracy)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = accuracy, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Accuracy on the held-out person") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal()
```

Accuracy on an unseen person averages `r pct(mean(loso_accuracy), 0)`, far
below the `r pct(accuracy, 1)` for known people. For
`r sum(loso_accuracy < always_a)` of the six it is worse than always guessing
class A. The likely reason, not tested here, is that raw readings depend on the
person as well as on the technique, through body size, strength and how the
sensors sat on them. If so, a forest trained on raw readings learns in part
what each of the six people looks like. That is harmless for the quiz, but a
real coaching app would need more than six people in training, calibration for
each new user, or features that describe whole repetitions rather than single
readings.

## Predictions for the 20 test cases

The test rows get the same 52 predictors and are classified by the validated
random forest.

```{r predict}
test_pred <- predict(rf_fit, test[predictors])
knitr::kable(t(data.frame(problem = test$problem_id, prediction = test_pred)))
```

## Conclusion

A random forest on 52 raw sensor readings, with `mtry` =
`r rf_fit$bestTune$mtry` chosen by 5-fold cross-validation, classifies the five
curl techniques with `r pct(accuracy, 2)` accuracy on an untouched validation
set. The expected out-of-sample error is **`r pct(oos_error, 2)`** (95% CI
`r pct(1 - accuracy_ci[2], 2)` to `r pct(1 - accuracy_ci[1], 2)`) for new
readings from the six people in the study, which is the setting of the 20 test
cases. For a person outside the study, expect far more errors. Accuracy on a
left-out participant ranged from `r pct(min(loso_accuracy), 0)` to
`r pct(max(loso_accuracy), 0)`.

## Reference

Velloso, E., Bulling, A., Gellersen, H., Ugulino, W. and Fuks, H. (2013).
*Qualitative Activity Recognition of Weight Lifting Exercises.* Proceedings of
the 4th International Conference in Cooperation with SIGCHI (Augmented
Human '13). Stuttgart, Germany: ACM SIGCHI. Data from the
[Weight Lifting Exercise Dataset](http://web.archive.org/web/20161224072740/http:/groupware.les.inf.puc-rio.br/har),
